newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban said advancing after helpful mutiny.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban said advancing after helpful mutiny.

text.p: Afghanistan's dominant Taleban Islamic militia said on Monday its forces were advancing to take the northwestern province of Faryab after northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum lost control of it.
"The Taleban forces are chasing the defeated militia from different sides," the Taleban-controlled radio in the capital Kabul said.
"The Islamic forces launched an offensive on Dostum fronts, broke their resistance lines and advanced on Faryab," said the broadcast monitored in Islamabad.
Earlier, a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service said Dostum had lost control of Faryab province to pro-Taleban mutineers.

The forces led by dissident General Abdul Malik had launched a pro-Taleban revolt against four Dostum-held provinces -- Faryab, Samangan, Jowzjan and Balkh, of which Mazar-i-Sharif is the capital -- earlier on Monday, the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said.
It was not immediately clear what had happened to Dostum in the uprising and there was no word on his whereabouts.
AIP said that Malik, a brother of Rasul Pahlivan, a powerful Dostum commander assassinated in Mazar-i-Sharif last year, had switched loyalties to the purist Islamic Taleban militia.
It said Malik had publicly announced support for the Taleban on Monday. Malik also said he had captured 5,000 Dostum soldiers and two northern provinces, but it was not clear which ones.
He vowed to keep up the struggle against Dostum, saying the tough Uzbek leader was "against a united Afghanistan".

Witnesses in Maimana, capital of Faryab province, about 250 km (156 miles) west of Dostum's bastion of Mazar-i-Sharif, said Dostum portraits had been removed and white flags were flying from government buildings to signify support for the Taleban.
"Dostum's forces appear to have brought the situation under control in Mazar-i-Sharif this (Monday) afternoon," AIP said.
It said Faryab province was in Malik's hands, but had no immediate word on the situation in Samangan or Jowzjan.
A senior Taleban official based in Kandahar, Wakil Ahmad, told AIP that the uprising had been planned jointly with Malik and the decision to launch it had been taken on Sunday.
The Taleban, who control the Afghan capital Kabul and more than two thirds of the country, have been trying to oust Dostum and other opposition leaders from northern provinces.

AIP mentioned reports that former Herat provincial governor Ismail Khan, who has been fighting the Taleban in northwest Afghanistan, had been arrested by Malik's forces along with eight of his men, but said it could not confirm them.

Aid workers contacted in Mazar-i-Sharif, 300 km (200 miles) northwest of Kabul, said the city was calm but rumours were flying. They had no reports of fighting in the town itself. AIP said Dostum's troops had clashed with mutineers in one area.

U.N. officials in Islamabad said Dostum's security officers at Mazar-i-Sharif airport had asked the United Nations not to send any planes there between midday and 4 p.m. (0730 and 1130 GMT) for unexplained security reasons.
The revolt follows last week's killing in Mazar-i-Sharif of a senior commander in Dostum's militia, Mullah Abdur Rahman Haqqani, who was shot dead along with 10 bodyguards.
Haqqani, aged about 50, commanded 500 regular troops for Dostum, but could raise about 2,000 irregulars in time of need,
Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, was a key commander for the pro-communist government led by president Najibullah, who was hanged by the Taleban when they captured Kabul on September 27.
He formed a loose alliance with two other leaders after the fall of the capital and their forces have been locked in combat with the Taleban north of Kabul and in northwest Afghanistan.

In April 1992, he switched sides to support mujahideen guerrilla groups that had battled Soviet troops occupying Afghanistan in the 1980s. Dostum's backing enabled the mujahideen to take over Kabul from Najibullah.
In January 1994, he allied with Hezb-i-Islami leader Gulbuddin Hekmatyar to stage an abortive coup attempt in the Afghan capital against then-president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Dostum was given the defence ministry in a new government formed by Rabbani in Mazar-i-Sharif earlier this month, but no post was announced for Ahmad Shah Masood, Rabbani's former military chief and a key member of the anti-Taleban alliance.
